ontology.name: Elements of Software
ontology.description: A reusable reference model for common SaaS and business-application concepts. It demonstrates parties instead of person-shaped duplicates, roles as reified states rather than entity types, one Task that nests, pipelines as properties rather than entity-type chains, and views, automations, permissions and audit events as first-class records. Software agents are modeled as parties alongside people and organizations.

entityTypes.name: Party
entityTypes.description: Anyone who can act: a person, an organization, or a software agent. Relations that any actor may hold point here once — assign a Task to a Party and all three kinds qualify. This single abstraction removes most person-shaped duplicate entity types from a schema.

properties.name: partyId
properties.description: One identifier for every kind of actor — person, organization or agent

entityTypes.name: Person
entityTypes.description: A human being. Note the modeling choice: an email address is a property of a Person; an email you send is an Interaction. Same word, two different kinds of thing.

properties.name: emailAddress
properties.description: An address is a property; a message sent to it is an Interaction

entityTypes.name: Organization
entityTypes.description: A company, institution, or other legal actor. Company, Account and Vendor are not three entity types — they are one Organization playing three different Roles.

entityTypes.name: Agent
entityTypes.description: A software actor. Modeled as a Party, not a feature: an agent holds tasks, sends interactions, and appears in the audit trail like anyone else. Every agent is operated by some Party — autonomy with a named principal.

properties.name: model
properties.description: The underlying model or runtime this agent runs on

properties.name: autonomyLevel
properties.description: How far the agent may act before a person confirms

entityTypes.name: Role
entityTypes.description: Lead, Customer, Vendor, Employee — not entity types, but roles a Party plays for a while, in the context of some Organization. Reifying the role keeps one Person one node while their relationships change. Promoting roles to entity types is the most common modeling mistake in business software.

properties.name: kind
properties.description: The role names that business software usually promotes to entity types

entityTypes.name: Team
entityTypes.description: An organizational unit that owns work. People are members; teams belong to an Organization.

entityTypes.name: Project
entityTypes.description: A bounded body of work with an owner and a lifecycle. Tasks belong to it; documents attach to it.

entityTypes.name: Task
entityTypes.description: A unit of work. One entity type with a parent relation replaces Task and Subtask — nesting is a relationship, not a new kind of thing. Assigned to a Party, so a person, a team's org, or an agent can hold it.

properties.name: status
properties.description: Lifecycle as a property, not an entity type per state

entityTypes.name: Document
entityTypes.description: Doc, File, Note and Template are formats of one thing: authored content that attaches to work. The kind property distinguishes them; four entity types would not.

properties.name: kind
properties.description: Doc, File, Note, Template: formats of one thing

entityTypes.name: Product
entityTypes.description: What you sell. A Service is a Product you cannot drop on your foot; a Plan is a Product that recurs. One entity type, a kind property, and a price.

properties.name: kind
properties.description: A Service is a Product you cannot drop on your foot; a Plan is a Product that recurs

entityTypes.name: Deal
entityTypes.description: A potential transaction moving through a pipeline. The pipeline lives in the stage property — modeling Lead, Opportunity and Deal as separate entity types forces a migration every time a prospect advances.

properties.name: stage
properties.description: The pipeline as a property — advancing a deal is an update, not a migration

entityTypes.name: Subscription
entityTypes.description: An ongoing agreement binding a Party to a Product over time. The recurring-revenue chain reads directly off the graph: Subscription is billed by Invoices, Invoices are settled by Payments.

entityTypes.name: Invoice
entityTypes.description: A demand for money owed under a Subscription. Has identity, lifecycle, and legal weight — a real entity, not a report.

entityTypes.name: Payment
entityTypes.description: Money actually moving. Settles an Invoice; the invoice-to-payment relation is where reconciliation lives.

entityTypes.name: Interaction
entityTypes.description: An email, call, meeting or chat message: one entity type, a channel property. Splitting these into four entity types duplicates every relation they share — participants, timestamps, the deal they concern.

properties.name: channel
properties.description: Email, call, meeting, chat — a property, not four entity types

entityTypes.name: SavedView
entityTypes.description: A Kanban board is not a thing in your domain — it is a way of looking at things. But a SAVED view is a real record: it has an owner, a filter, and a layout. The layout belongs in a property; the view belongs in the schema.

properties.name: layout
properties.description: Kanban, list, calendar: ways of looking, so they live in a property

entityTypes.name: Automation
entityTypes.description: A rule is data: when trigger, if condition, then action. Storing it as an entity means it can be owned, versioned, disabled and audited — automation you can hold accountable.

properties.name: trigger
properties.description: When: the event that wakes this rule

properties.name: condition
properties.description: If: the test that must hold before it acts

entityTypes.name: Permission
entityTypes.description: A grant of access: which Party may do how much to what kind of resource. Modeled as an entity so access is queryable — who can edit this, and since when.

properties.name: resourceKind
properties.description: What kind of thing the grant covers, e.g. Project or Document

entityTypes.name: AuditEvent
entityTypes.description: The append-only memory of the system: who did what, when, to what. In software where agents act alongside people, the audit trail is what makes trust checkable rather than assumed.

properties.name: verb
properties.description: What was done: created, updated, deleted, approved, exported

relationships.name: operated by
relationships.description: Every agent answers to a principal

relationships.name: plays
relationships.description: Party plays Role: the pattern that replaces Lead, Customer and Vendor as entity types

relationships.name: at
relationships.description: A role is played somewhere: you are a customer AT a company, an employee AT another

relationships.name: subtask of
relationships.description: The self-relation that deletes the Subtask entity type: nesting is a relationship, not a kind

relationships.name: assigned to
relationships.description: Assigned to a Party — so a person or an agent can hold it, with no schema change

relationships.name: authored by
relationships.description: People and agents both write; the byline points at Party

relationships.name: with
relationships.description: The counterparty — a person or an organization, which is why it points at Party

relationships.name: involves
relationships.description: Participants are Parties: a meeting of two people and an agent is one Interaction

relationships.name: maintained by
relationships.description: Every rule has an owner you can ask why

relationships.name: creates
relationships.description: When it fires, work appears — and the AuditEvent says so

relationships.name: granted to
relationships.description: Access is granted to Parties — people and agents under one policy model

relationships.name: performed by
relationships.description: Whoever acted — person, organization or agent — the trail reads the same
